t.tashkurgan@37.8,75.2:
Tashkurgan is a small town in the far west of China's Xinjiang region, high on a plateau among the Pamirs at roughly three thousand metres. After crossing the Khunjerab Pass, at about 4,700 metres one of the highest paved border crossings in the world, it is the first real place you reach on the Chinese side. For anyone coming up the Karakoram Highway from Pakistan, it feels like arriving at the end of the earth and the beginning of a new one.

The people here are mostly Tajik, an Iranian-speaking mountain people quite unlike the Han Chinese or the Uyghurs of the plains below, and the county is officially a Tajik autonomous one. The faces, the clothes, the singing and the drum dances all point toward Central Asia. Above the town stand the remains of an old stone fort, and the name itself is thought to mean stone fortress. For centuries this was a stop on the Silk Road, where caravans from Kashgar and from the passes to the south exchanged goods and news before the next stage of the trip.

The setting is wide and austere. The valley opens into broad pastures edged by bare brown mountains, with snow on the higher summits and wind that comes through in cold bursts. Yaks and camels graze along the road. Further north, toward Kashgar, the highway runs past the vast Karakul Lake and the huge, glaciated mass of Muztagh Ata, over 7,500 metres, a mountain that turns pink at dusk and appears to float above the water.

The road itself is generally good asphalt, wide and well engineered by Chinese crews, though high altitude, cold nights and landslides can interrupt travel. The border crossing is seasonal, typically closed through the deep winter, and crossing it with a foreign motorcycle involves official permission and arrangements that need to be made well ahead, so this is not a place to improvise.

Tashkurgan has the facilities of a border town: fuel, simple restaurants, guesthouses and a market. Altitude matters, so take it gently, drink water, and expect a headache the first night if you came up fast. The lamb noodles and fresh bread are good, and the tea is hot.
t.khunjerab pass@36.9,75.4:
Khunjerab is the top of the road, and the road, in this case, is the Karakoram Highway. At 4,693 metres, the pass sits on the border between Pakistan and China and is the highest paved international crossing in the world. There is not much to see except a white arch, a barrier, a few border markers and an enormous sense of space. The surrounding hills are high, bare and rounded, covered in snow for most of the year, and the sky seems closer than anywhere else. The name itself comes from local words meaning something like the valley of blood, though the story behind it is disputed.

The pass is open to traffic only for part of the year, usually from the spring until late autumn, when snow blocks it. Even in July, the temperature can drop below freezing at night, and the wind is cold and constant. Altitude is a real problem. Riders arriving quickly from lower levels may feel headaches, breathlessness and nausea, and a carburetted bike will run noticeably rough in the thin air. Take it slowly, drink a lot, and do not stay too long at the top if you feel unwell.

The area is protected as the Khunjerab National Park, one of the highest in the world, home to Marco Polo sheep, with their huge spiralling horns, as well as ibex, blue sheep, snow leopards and Himalayan marmots. Yaks graze the high pastures in summer, and on the road up you can see herders' stone huts. The long ride from Sost, the last Pakistani town and customs post, takes you through a stark, glaciated landscape, past peaks over six thousand metres and frozen streams.

Crossing into China is not possible for an independent rider without a lot of arrangement, usually requiring permits, a guide and specific paperwork, so for most, the pass is the end of the road. Sost has fuel, simple food and the immigration office, and you should fill up there. There is nothing at the top beyond a checkpoint and, occasionally, a small tea stall. Pack warm clothes, as the descent is long and chilly, and expect the road to be rough in places after the winter, with potholes and washed-out sections.
t.karakoram highway point 8@36.9,75.4:
Khunjerab Pass, at 4,693 metres, is the highest paved international border crossing in the world, and it sits on the roof between Pakistan and China. The road climbs from Sost in a long series of gentle switchbacks, the tarmac smooth and wide, and the valley opens into a bleak, beautiful world of rounded brown mountains, snow patches and a sky that looks very close. A white gate marks the border and a modest stone sign says what you need to know.

The name means roughly valley of blood or the place where the stream flows, depending on who is translating, and the pass has been used by caravans for thousands of years. Marco Polo sheep, with their huge curving horns, live in the national park that surrounds the road, and with patience you may see ibex, marmots and, rarely, a snow leopard. Yaks graze in summer.

Be realistic about the ride. Oxygen is thin, so the bike runs rich and you feel it too: slow down, breathe, and take breaks. Weather can swing from sunshine to sleet inside an hour. The pass is open only in the warmer part of the year, generally from spring until late autumn, and it closes for snow, so check dates. Do not expect services on the pass itself beyond a seasonal tea stall.

The highway here is a monument to hard labour. Pakistani and Chinese work crews built it through some of the worst terrain on earth, and a memorial to the Chinese workers who died stands in Gilgit. Standing at the gate, with the road continuing north into Xinjiang, you can feel the line of history running through the stones.

Wear a warm jacket, even in July. The wind is bitter, and the cold sets in fast when cloud covers the sun. A short stay is the sensible plan, so take a photograph at the sign, enjoy the silence, and then roll back downhill toward the green of Hunza, where air feels rich and warm.
t.karakoram highway point 9@37.8,75.2:
Tashkurgan lies on the Chinese side of the Pamir, a small town in a wide, high valley at about 3,100 metres, with bare mountains around it and a river flat and braided along the bottom. It is the capital of the Tashkurgan Tajik Autonomous County, and its people are Tajik in language and culture, related to the Persian-speaking peoples of the Pamirs rather than to the Han majority of China. Faces, clothes, and music reflect that, and so does the food.

Above the town stands the Stone City, a ruined fortress on a hill whose walls date back many centuries, and which gave Tashkurgan its name, as the Turkic word means stone fortress. Traders on the Silk Road stopped here between Kashgar and the passes to India and Persia, and some scholars have thought the town to be the Stone Tower mentioned in ancient geography. The view from the ruins over the grassland, with the white wall of Muztagh Ata faintly visible on a clear day further north, makes the climb worthwhile.

For a rider, this is a different world of rules. In China, foreign visitors on motorcycles generally need special permits, a local guide and a temporary licence, and arrangements must usually be made well in advance through an agency. Do not expect to roll across the border on a whim. For those who arrange it, the road from Khunjerab descends smoothly into the Pamir plateau, with wide tarmac and long sight lines, and the climate is dry, cold and windy.

Tashkurgan has fuel, restaurants serving lamb, flatbread, noodles and yak yoghurt, and a number of hotels. The town is also the site of the immigration post for the pass, and opening hours follow Beijing time, which sits several hours ahead of local daylight, so the sun rises and sets late in the day. Expect long, bright evenings in summer.

The region is open to travellers mostly in the warmer months, because winter snows close the pass. The grassland comes alive in summer, with herders, sheep and yaks, and, further north, the great turquoise lake of Karakul draws visitors. This is the end of the Pakistan highway and the beginning of the long road to Kashgar.
